Imagine we’re planning a mission to the Moon’s south pole. Our first question is where the spacecraft can land. Our second is when conditions are best for landing there.

Even if the terrain looks suitable for landing, the spacecraft could spend long periods in shadow on the dates we choose. Nearby ridges can also affect when the spacecraft has a direct line of sight to Earth.

We developed ALPHA LUNAR to answer these questions together. We brought NASA’s open lunar data into a single 3D atlas.

Once users select a region and a date range, they can explore the terrain, sunlight conditions, and Earth visibility on a single screen. They can then compare different regions or date ranges using the same mission criteria.

What does the mission team see?

ALPHA LUNAR helps mission teams assess where and when to land at the Moon’s south pole.

The team selects a site and a date range in the 3D atlas. On a single screen, they can see how steep the terrain is, how long the spacecraft could receive sunlight, and when it would have a direct line of sight to Earth.

They can then compare sites and dates to decide which options to investigate further.

What data did we use?

We used open data from NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) to model the Moon’s terrain. We combined that terrain model with NASA JPL’s SPICE data to calculate when the Sun and Earth would be visible from the selected site during the chosen date range.

We turned NASA’s open data into a tool that helps mission teams assess a practical question: “Can we operate at this site during this time window?”


Science

  • Terrain assessment
  • Illumination analysis
  • Visibility analysis
  • Access to ice resources
  • Sunrise, sunset, Earthrise, and Earthset
  • Sunlight duration
  • Communication windows with Earth
  • Ranking of evidence for water ice

Technology

  • 3D lunar atlas
  • Power planning
  • Communications planning
  • Landing site and date comparisons
  • Scenario analysis with Moon AI
  • Reports with source citations

Data

  • Landing sites
  • Orbital and positional data (ephemerides)
  • Terrain data
  • Water ice findings
  • Positions of the Sun and Earth in the lunar sky
